title: Environmental stressors, urban design and planning: implications for human behaviour and health
review_question: How do environmental stressors (crowding and noise) in indoor settings (residential, school, work, commuting) impact human behavior and health, and how can urban design and planning mitigate these effects?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Studies written in English using human subjects, primarily searched via Google Scholar. Search terms included 'crowding', 'density', 'residential crowding', 'classroom crowding', 'workplace crowding', 'privacy in office', 'office type', 'commute crowding', 'chronic noise', 'environmental noise', 'residential noise and children', 'noise and blood pressure', 'classroom noise', 'office noise', 'open office noise', 'transportation noise and commute', with 'stress' added to some terms. 'Neighbourhood quality' was also used. Studies from other cultures were not excluded, but most reviewed were from Western countries.

synthesis_conclusions: Crowding and noise are significant environmental stressors that negatively impact human health and behavior, including physiological responses (blood pressure, cortisol), mental health, cognitive performance, and academic achievement.
High density in residential and classroom settings can reduce caregiver responsiveness and engagement with children, mediating adverse outcomes.
Chronic noise interferes with cognitive performance and children's cognitive development.
Good acoustic design (minimizing sound transmission, optimizing reverberation time) can lessen noise and potentially crowding.
Immediate access to semi-public spaces or 'third places' can reduce noise and crowding, and is critical for coping with residential crowding.
Natural elements, aesthetically-pleasing urban design, and pedestrian/bicycling-friendly streets can mitigate crowding and urban noise, and help break continuous exposure.
Exposure to multiple stressors can exacerbate negative consequences, and the interaction between interior and exterior environmental quality is significant for stress outcomes.
evidence_gaps: The interdependence between built environments across scales is poorly understood.
Psychologists' traditional focus on laboratory settings makes it difficult for designers/planners to use insights in practice.
The critical experience of transitions over time and across settings is given inadequate attention in environment and empirical research.
Few studies have examined how architectural design moderates adverse impacts of high sound and interior density levels.
It is unknown whether crowding itself exacerbates noise in residential settings.
Few studies have examined indoor-generated noise in residential settings.
Little is known about sound attenuation of traffic noise.
Scant research has looked into the effects of sound barrier walls on annoyance, and none have examined their potential mitigation on cognitive functions or physiological responses.
It is unknown how household crowding interacted with school crowding in the Project STAR study.
Studies of new types of hybrid office designs are limited and have generated mixed results.
Office studies focus on interior environments without consideration of how they are nested within building types or neighbourhoods.
No studies about the relationships among sound levels, durations, and stress during commutes have been identified.

No studies have examined if subway seating patterns (e.g., middle seats taken in Seoul vs. avoided in New York) are due to train car design, familiarity with high-density residential life, or cultural norms.
Future studies regarding seat design in public transportation are encouraged.
Both environmental psychology and design and planning research ought to more thoroughly investigate design properties as potential moderators of environmental stress effects.
Few studies have examined the connections between building design and outdoor surroundings.
Few studies have looked into the interaction between interior and exterior environments regarding stress.

moderators.variable: House type (large multi-dwelling units vs. single-family/row houses)
moderators.effect: Mental health was worse for children in more crowded large multi-dwelling units.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Children in large multi-dwelling units experienced worse mental health outcomes from crowding.

moderators.effect: Neighbourhood quality can moderate housing characteristics to change its impacts on residents.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Poor quality housing in a poor quality neighbourhood produces significantly more stress than either alone.

moderators.effect: Household density increased externalizing behaviours only among boys; high household density was associated with boys' high blood pressure and girls' learned helplessness.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Males may have greater personal space relative to females. Road traffic noise increased blood pressure in males but not females. Higher street noise lowered executive functioning only among boys.

moderators.effect: Children chronically exposed to noise appear to learn to tune out auditory stimuli. Noise effects on children's mental health are less clear. Noise exposure may not produce additional damage once children reach secondary school.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Children living near Munich Airport reported lower quality of life after opening. Noise effects on reading comprehension were stronger among older elementary students. Irrelevant speech was detrimental for recognition memory among adults over 35.

moderators.effect: Night-time aircraft noise elevated blood pressure in adults who had lived in the same residence five years or longer. In Sweden, those who had lived at the same residence over 10 years showed stronger effects.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Longer residence duration amplified noise effects.

moderators.effect: Acoustic design can be important in primary environments (open offices, open classrooms).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Proper acoustic design can mitigate negative effects of noise.

moderators.variable: Setting (e.g., residence vs. school, work vs. recreation)
moderators.effect: The perception of high density varies by type of setting (e.g., night clubs vs. residential).
moderators.subgroup_effects: Noise sources and their annoyance vary by setting (e.g., human-generated sounds indoors vs. traffic noise outdoors).

limitations: The review primarily focused on studies conducted in Western countries, despite not explicitly excluding other cultures.
The review did not exclude studies conducted in other cultures; however, most studies reviewed were conducted in Western countries.
The paper discusses office settings instead of workplace in general, which may differ from other workplace types.

Some studies on residential crowding had a limitation in their prescriptive temporal sequence (crowding → diminished parent-child interaction → adverse child outcomes) and were cross-sectional, suggesting a need for more rigorous longitudinal approaches.

Many noise and children's reading studies used large samples pre-screened for normal auditory activity and relied on noise assessment data (e.g., Leq(A) contour maps) without adjusting for individual-level environmental variables or building attributes, potentially leading to imprecise estimates of actual exposures.
Few residential-noise studies measure indoor sound levels directly.
Studies on new types of office design are limited and have generated mixed results.
Office studies focus on interior environments without considering how they are nested within building types or neighbourhoods.
